name: The Trials That Judged an Age
description: Courtroom dramas from Athens to Nuremberg and beyond: what Socrates, Joan of Arc, Dreyfus, Mandela and others tell us about justice and power.

checkpoints.name: Conscience in the dock
checkpoints.note: Athens tried Socrates and condemned him to death in 399 BCE. In 1431 Joan of Arc was tried by a Church court and burned, and in 1535 Thomas More was convicted in England and executed.

checkpoints.name: Plots, heresy and kings
checkpoints.note: Guy Fawkes and the Gunpowder Plot ended in trials, and the Church tried Galileo in the Galileo affair. In 1649 a court tried King Charles I, and in 1692 and 1693 the Salem witch trials ended in executions.

checkpoints.name: Scandals and show trials
checkpoints.note: The Dreyfus affair split France, and Oscar Wilde's trials ended his career. In 1925 John Scopes was tried for teaching evolution, and in the Moscow trials Stalin's rivals confessed and were condemned.

checkpoints.name: Judging the war and the law
checkpoints.note: The Nuremberg trials and the Tokyo trials judged leaders of Germany and Japan. The Supreme Court ruled against school segregation in Brown v. Board of Education, and Israel tried Adolf Eichmann in 1961.

checkpoints.name: Power on trial
checkpoints.note: At the Rivonia Trial Nelson Mandela was sentenced to life in prison. The Watergate scandal ended with the resignation of Richard Nixon, and in 1998 the House voted to impeach Bill Clinton, whom the Senate then acquitted.
